title: Slack Wrike Integration: How to Set It Up (2026 Guide)
summary: Set up a slack wrike integration by building two message workflows. One workflow sends Slack messages to Wrike, the other posts Wrike updates to Slack.
body_markdown:
## Other Tools for Slack and Wrike and When Activepieces Fits


If you want the duplicate-skip logic and the whole workflow on infrastructure you control,[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/pieces/slack) fits, since its MIT-licensed core can be self-hosted. If Wrike's own Slack integration or a hosted tool already covers your case, use that instead.


### Native apps and other automation tools


Start with what is already in your workspace. If Wrike's built-in Slack integration does the one thing you need, such as posting task updates to a channel, it costs you nothing to set up.


The limit is that you get its behavior as shipped. You can't add a step that checks a stored message timestamp before a task is created.


Below is a comparison of Zapier, Make and n8n against Activepieces, whose core is MIT-licensed, on Wrike and Slack triggers and actions, free tier, open source and self-hosting.


On both apps, Zapier lists the \[First product\] lists the most triggers and actions, Make lists fewer of each, and n8n lists fewer triggers than Make but more actions.


Your text started mid-sentence, so I left the first product name as a placeholder. If you send the full original, I'll keep its numbers and names and neutralise any superlative in the opening clause.


Read it as a coverage check: whichever tool you pick, confirm the specific trigger your workflow starts from exists before you build.


For Activepieces, the figures to check are 750 integrations counted from the open-source monorepo, an MIT-licensed core, and unlimited flows on the Free plan, which includes 1,000 credits a month.


Where a tool lacks a Wrike action, a gap costs you one call to the Wrike API rather than a dead end, because every tool in the table has an HTTP request step.


### When open source, self-hosting and unlimited steps matter


You lean toward Activepieces in three situations. First, Wrike task data passes through the automation host, and your policy says it must stay on servers you run. Activepieces has an MIT-licensed core and can be self-hosted, so that's possible.


Second, your workflows are small but chatty, with a dedupe check, a lookup and a post on every run. On a self-hosted install no vendor meters those steps, though you take on the upkeep of the server, upgrades and backups.


Third, you want to read the integration's source when a trigger behaves oddly. That matters on day three, when a Slack event fires twice and you need to see why.


For the duplicate problem specifically, the dedupe check is just one more step in a small workflow, and on Activepieces a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, so the check adds nothing to the Free plan's 1,000 credits a month.


The HTTP request step covers any Wrike field the integration doesn't expose.


### Build the chat-to-task workflow with deduplication


Build the chat-to-task flow first, because its dedupe check is the part most likely to go wrong. Use the Slack trigger, add the storage lookup for the timestamp, and branch so a repeat ends the run. Only the new-message path reaches the Wrike create-task action.


Once that runs cleanly against a test channel, build the task-to-channel flow as a separate workflow.
